model.name: Greene2025 - Hypoxia- and biomechanically driven EMT model

body.p: This model expands our "Regan2022 - Mechanosensitive EMT model with autocrine TGFbeta signaling" model (MODEL2208050002) with hypoxic signaling. It reproduces hypoxia-driven cell cycle arrest, the need for moderate Hif1-alpha activity for cell cycle progression, the mechanosensitive (density-dependent) nature of hypoxia-driven EMT. The model explores the succession of microenvironments and phenotype changes a metastatic cancer cell encounters from a primary tumor to a secondary site.

xhtml:body.xhtml:p: The \textit{CellDensity\_High} node in our model represents an extracellular environment with high enough cell density to block cell spreading. This input node is self-sustaining in the absence of \textit{in silico} perturbation.

The \textit{CellDensity\_Low} node represents an environment with cell density comparable to the edge of a monolayer, where cells can maintain strong adhesions with each other but are also able to spread and polarize horizontally.

The \textit{Sfiff\_ECM} input node represents access to a very stiff extracellular matrix that promotes / supports stress fiber formation sufficiently to place no limitation on a cell’s capacity to proliferate ( $>$ 100 kPa) \cite{maMechanotransductionAnoikisDeath2008}. This input node is self-sustaining in the absence of \textit{in silico} perturbation.

The \textit{ECM} input node represents access to a very soft extracellular matrix that does not support cell spreading or stress fiber formation ( $<$ 0.5 kPa), but does support anchorage-dependent survival signaling \cite{maMechanotransductionAnoikisDeath2008}. This input node is self-sustaining in the absence of a stiff \textit{ECM} (or \textit{in silico} perturbation), and overridden to an ON state otherwise by \textit{Stiff\_ECM}.

The \textit{GF} node represents an extracellular environment with low levels of growth factors capable of sustaining survival signaling. Thus, the \textit{GF} input node is self-sustaining in the absence of \textit{in silico} perturbation.

The \textit{GF\textsubscript{High}} node in our model represents an extracellular environment with saturating levels of growth factors; this input node is self-sustaining in the absence of \textit{in silico} perturbation.

The ON state of the \textit{RTK} node in our model represents basal growth receptor activation (required to keep a normal cell alive). Thus it requires the absence of \textit{CAD} and at least low growth levels of growth factors in the extracellular environment \cite{Lemmon:2010bq}.

{\textit{Shc} is ON when \textit{RTK}s are activated by high levels of extracellular growth factors (capable of driving proliferation) \cite{ahmedInsightsShcFamily2017} {or \textit{TGF$\beta$} activates \textit{T$\beta$RI-T$\beta$RII} \cite{zhangNonSmadPathwaysTGFbeta2009}}, and its recruitment is aided by active \textit{Src} kinase \cite{schlaepferMultipleGrb2mediatedIntegrinstimulated1998} or focal adhesion kinase (\textit{FAK}) \cite{schlaepferMultipleGrb2mediatedIntegrinstimulated1998}. The two mediators of integrin signaling appears to be able to act independently, forming two parallel links between integrin signaling and full \textit{RTK} activation \cite{schlaepferMultipleGrb2mediatedIntegrinstimulated1998}.}

\textit{Grb2} is recruited to \textit{RTKs} {or \textit{TGF$\beta$}} receptors upon ligand binding and subsequent recruitment of \textit{Shc} adaptors \cite{Uzman:2001iy, zhangNonSmadPathwaysTGFbeta2009}.
\textit{RTK}-bound \textit{Grb2} recruits \textit{SOS}, a guanine nucleotide–exchange protein (GEF) that converts inactive \textit{Ras} to its active GTP-bound form \cite{Uzman:2001iy}.

\textit{Ras} activation requires the GEF activity of \textit{SOS} and the \textit{RTK}-linked (active) adaptor protein \textit{Grb2} \cite{Uzman:2001iy} and \textit{Src} \cite{belschesRoleCSrcTyrosine1997,rocksAcylationCycleRegulates2005}. In addition to aiding sustained \textit{Ras/Raf-1} signaling, \textit{Src} may also physically link \textit{IQGAP1} to \textit{RTKs} such as \textit{VEGFR2} \cite{meyerIQGAP1dependentSignalingPathway2008}. \textit{IQGAP1}, in turn, serves a scaffold for \textit{MAPK} and \textit{PI3K} signaling \cite{choiAktionIQGAP1Control2017}, leading us to link its activation at the leading edge. In contrast, \textit{Merlin} blocks \textit{Ras} activation at sites that link focal adhesions and actin filaments to \textit{MAPK} signaling \cite{morrisonMerlinNeurofibromatosisType2007}. Here we assume that concentrated \textit{IQGAP1} at the leading edge can override remaining \textit{Merlin} activity in the rest of the cell. Alternatively, high levels of \textit{$\beta$-catenin} can also sustain \textit{Ras} by protecting it from lysosomal degradation \cite{jeonAxinInhibitsExtracellular2007}.

\textit{Raf} is active in response to \textit{Ras} activity in the absence of \textit{Caspase 3}. As active \textit{Raf-1} is continuously dephosphorylated and bound by \textit{14-3-3}, which translocates it to the cytoplasm from the plasma membrane (not modeled explicitly), ongoing \textit{Ras} activity \cite{Chang:2003cy} and lack of \textit{SPRY2} inhibition \cite{yusoffSprouty2InhibitsRas2002,bradySprouty2AssociationBRaf2009} are necessary to keep \textit{Raf} ON.
\textit{Raf} phosphorylates and activates the \textit{MEK} kinase \cite{Chang:2003cy}.

The \textit{ERK} kinase is active when phoisphotylated by \textit{MEK} \cite{Chang:2003cy} and allowed to translocate to the nucleus in the absence of \textit{BIK} \cite{Mebratu:2008gn}. {Here we assume that in the presence of \textit{DUSP4} \cite{rameshTGFvMediatedBIM2008,wildeySmad3PotentiatesTransforming2003}, \textit{ERK} activity can be maintained /compensated by either strong focal adhesion assembly (\textit{FocalAdhesions} node) \cite{yinGIT1ScaffoldERK12005}, or high levels of $\beta$-\textit{catenin} \cite{yunBothERKWnt2005}. }

Our model assumes that \textit{mTORC2} is active in quiescent cells with basal levels of \textit{PI3K} activity leading to basal \textit{PIP3} generation. Alternatively, the absence of high growth factor-stimulated \textit{mTORC1} and \textit{S6K1} can also increase \textit{mTORC2} activity.

In our model, basal \textit{PI3K} activity can be maintained by active \textit{RTK}s \cite{Lemmon:2010bq}, active \textit{Ras} \cite{RodriguezViciana:1994kn,Gupta:2007dw}, {or active \textit{T$\beta$RI-T$\beta$RII} \cite{zhangSignalingInterplayTransforming2013}}. In addition, survival signalling via \textit{PI3K} requires anchorage-dependent signals via active \textit{FAK} \cite{khwajaMatrixAdhesionRas1997} or via \textit{Src}-mediated blocking of basal \textit{PTEN} activity (not modeled explicitly) \cite{luSrcFamilyProteintyrosine2003}.
In our model, PIP3 is ON as a result of basal or high \textit{PI3K} activity.
\textit{PDK1} enzyme activation requires active (at least basal) \textit{PI3K} and \textit{PIP3} \cite{Manning:2017di}.

Basal \textit{AKT1} activity in our model requires the absence of \textit{Caspase 3}, the availability of at least basal levels of \textit{PIP3}, and phosphorylation by \textit{PDK1} or \textit{mTORC2}. In contrast, full mitogen-stimulated \textit{AKT1} activation requires phosphorylation by both (see \textit{AKT\_H}) \cite{Manning:2017di}.

As \textit{YAP} is a transcriptional inducer of \textit{p110} subunits \cite{linPi3kcbLinksHippoYAP2015} and their expression is low in high cell density areas where \textit{YAP} activity is suppressed \cite{Yuan:2011dm}, here we assume that high \textit{p110} expression requires active \textit{YAP}. In order to capture the cyclic dynamics of \textit{p110} protein expression, we make the assumption that high \textit{p110} protein levels can be induced by \textit{FoxO3} in the absence of the growth factor-activated \textit{Nedd4L} ubiquitin ligase. Once present, high \textit{p110} can be maintained by \textit{FoxO3} transcription, or the absence of activated \textit{Nedd4L}.

Full, peak-level activation of \textit{PI3K} requires high levels of \textit{p110} protein, basal \textit{PI3K} activation, active \textit{Ras}, and active \textit{RTK}s {or \textit{T$\beta$RI-T$\beta$RII}}. As the ON-state of \textit{Ras} in our model represents strong \textit{Ras} activation in the presence of proliferation-inducing (high) growth factors, \textit{PI3K\_H} activation can only occur in these conditions. In addition, a reduction of cytoplasmic \textit{PTEN} levels is also required for peak \textit{PI3K} activity.

In contact to basal \textit{AKT1}, high \textit{AKT1} activity in our model requires basal \textit{AKT1} (\textit{AKT\_B}), the ongoing presence of high \textit{p110} protein levels along with active \textit{PI3K\_H} and \textit{PIP3}. In addition this maximal \textit{AKT1} activation requires phosphorylation by both \textit{PDK1} and \textit{mTORC2}, , as well as either active \textit{Ras} \cite{Manning:2017di} or \textit{PAK1} \cite{higuchiScaffoldingFunctionPAK2008}. {In response to \textit{TGF$\beta$}, high \textit{AKT1} activity can also be induced by \textit{PI3K} and the \textit{ILK-Rictor} complex; the latter capable of replacing \textit{mTORC2} to supply S473 phosphorylation of \textit{AKT1} \cite{serranoRoleIntegrinlinkedKinase2013,mcdonaldRictorIntegrinlinkedKinase2008}}.

In order to account for all the influences on \textit{FoxO3} activity, we used the following logic. In the absence of basal or high \textit{AKT1} as well as \textit{ERK}, \textit{FoxO3} remains active. In addition, \textit{FoxO3} can overcame peak (\textit{AKT\_H}) activation only if no other inhibitor is present and \textit{AKT\_B} is OFF (indicating that \textit{AKT1} levels are falling). Finally, the joint activity of \textit{ERK} and \textit{Plk1} can also block \textit{FoxO3}.

Peak activation of \textit{PLC}$\gamma$ requires active an \textit{RTK} receptor node bound by active \textit{Grb2}, as well as high \textit{PI3K} activity (including high \textit{p110} availability and the presence of PIP3).

Membrane-bound, active \textit{PLC}$\gamma$ is responsible for converting phosphatidylinositol(4,5)P2 (\textit{PIP2}) to the second messenger inositol(1,4,5)P3 (\textit{IP3}) responsible for triggering a sudden \textit{Ca$^{2+}$} influx from the endoplasmic reticulum, along with \textit{DAG} (diacylglycerol, another second messenger) \cite{Gresset:2012hm}.

\textit{IP3} travels from the cell membrane to the endoplasmic reticulum where it opens \textit{IP3}-sensitive \textit{Ca$^{2+}$} channels, releasing a sudden \textit{Ca$^{2+}$} efflux from the ER into the cytosol \cite{Michell:1981th}.
Activation of \textit{Nedd4L} requires both \textit{Ca$^{2+}$} and \textit{IP3} binding \cite{Escobedo:2014dg}.
\textit{FoxO1} is transcriptionally active in the absence of peak \textit{AKT1} activation and \textit{Plk1} activity.

Our model requires both FoxOs to induce \textit{p21\textsuperscript{Cip1}} if \textit{Myc} is active and one of the two if \textit{Myc} is OFF {or \textit{FoxO} factors are aided by \textit{Smad} activity \cite{gomisFoxOSmadSynexpressionGroup2006}}. This is based on data showing that both \textit{FoxO3} and \textit{FoxO1} bind and induce the \textit{p21\textsuperscript{Cip1}} promoter and that loss of \textit{Myc} repression alone is not sufficient to induce \textit{p21\textsuperscript{Cip1}} \cite{seoaneIntegrationSmadForkhead2004}. Finally, high levels of \textit{ZEB1} repress \textit{p21\textsuperscript{Cip1}} mRNA expression \cite{huDeltaEF1PromotesBreast2010}.

Blocking \textit{TSC2} requires ongoing mitogen stimulation through \textit{AKT} and/or \textit{ERK}. In our model, \textit{TSC2} inhibition requires high (peak) \textit{AKT} activity, supported by either \textit{ERK} or basal \textit{AKT} (assuring that complete loss of \textit{AKT} activity is not impending) \cite{saxtonMTORSignalingGrowth2017}.

\textit{PRAS40} is inhibited by peak \textit{AKT1} activity aided by either basal \textit{AKT1} (meaning \textit{AKT\_H} is on its way down), or ongoing \textit{mTORC1} activation. Both \textit{AKT1} and \textit{mTORC1} phosphorylate \textit{PRAS40}, leading to its dissociation from \textit{mTORC1} \cite{wizaRolePRAS40Akt2012}.

Membrane-bound, active \textit{PLC}$\gamma$ is responsible for converting phosphatidylinositol(4,5)P2 (\textit{PIP2}) to the second messenger diacylglycerol (\textit{DAG}), along with \textit{IP3} \cite{Gresset:2012hm}.

\textit{PKC} (and \textit{DAG})-dependent activation of \textit{mTORC1} recruits \textit{mTORC1} to the site of \textit{Rheb} activity (to prenuclear lysosomes), while \textit{AKT} and \textit{ERK}-mediated \textit{TSC2} inhibition guarantees that \textit{Rheb} remains potent \cite{inokiRhebGTPaseDirect2003,liuCoordinatedActivationClassical2017,demetriadesLysosomalRecruitmentTSC22016}.

\textit{mTORC1} is activated by mitogenic signals via \textit{Rheb} in the absence of \textit{PRAS40}{\color{NavyBlue}, aided by metabolic changes mediated by proliferation-linked \textit{Hif1-$\alpha$} activation (modeled as the \textit{Hif1a\_basal} node)}. This, however, also requires inactivation of \textit{Merlin}, independently of \textit{RTK}-induced signals. In addition, \textit{E2F1} can promote \textit{mTORC1} activity{\color{NavyBlue}, likely aided by \textit{ERK}-mediated phosphorylation of it's \textit{Raptor} component}. Finally, the mitotic \textit{Cyclin B} and its \textit{Cdk1} kinase can also activate \textit{mTORC1}, aided by \textit{GSK3}.
\textit{S6K} is activated by \textit{mTORC1} in the absence of \textit{Caspase 3}.

{\textit{4EBP1}, or eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E-binding protein 1, binds and sequesters the initiation factor \textit{eIF4F} and thus limits translation. \textit{mTORC1} phosphorylates and deactivates \textit{4EBP} to upregulate protein biosynthesis \cite{saxtonMTORSignalingGrowth2017}. While in our previous models this protein was implicit along the \textit{mTORC1} $\rightarrow$ \textit{eIF4F} link \cite{sizekBooleanModelGrowth2019,gubermanBooleanModelAnchorage2020}, we include it here because \textit{TGF$\beta$} signaling induces \textit{4EBP1} via \textit{SMAD4} to block proliferative metabolism \cite{azar4EBP1TargetSmad42009}.}

\textit{eIF4E} is activated by \textit{mTORC1}-mediated repression {of \textit{4EBP1}, which normally binds to it and blocks its activity} \cite{saxtonMTORSignalingGrowth2017}. \textit{eIF4E} is cleaved and deactivated by \textit{Caspase 3} \cite{bushellCaspase3NecessarySufficient1999}.
\textit{GSK3} activity can be completely blocked by peak \textit{AKT} activation ( \textit{AKT\_H}), or by the joint action of \textit{S6K} and \textit{ERK}.

Integrins are a superfamily of heterodimeric cell adhesion receptors that bind to extracellular matrix ligands, cell-surface ligands, and soluble ligands. Upon ligand binding, integrins transduce biomechanical information to the cell interior \cite{takadaIntegrins2007}.

{Integrin-linked kinase \textit{ILK} interacts with the cytoplasmic domain of $\beta$1 integrins, and acrs as a scaffold connecting integrins to the actin cytoskeleton and other signalling pathways \cite{hanniganIntegrinlinkedKinaseCancer2005}.}

\textit{FAK} is activated at integrin-ECM attachment sites in the absence of \textit{Caspase 3}-mediated cleavage and \textit{Cyclin B/Cdk1} activity \cite{mitraFocalAdhesionKinase2005,gervaisCaspasesCleaveFocal1998,yamakitaDissociationFAKP1301999}.

\textit{Src} is activated by \textit{FAK} or \textit{RTKs} at sites of integrin-ECM {\color{NavyBlue} or cell-cell} attachments \cite{mitraIntegrinregulatedFAKSrcSignaling2006,bromannInterplaySrcFamily2004}, by \textit{TGF$\beta$} signaling \cite{ungefrorenDifferentialRolesSrc2011}{\color{NavyBlue}, or hypoxia and ROS \cite{daiCSrcRequiredHypoxiainduced2019,giannoniIntracellularReactiveOxygen2005}}. In addition, \textit{Cyclin B / Cdk1} phosphorylate \textit{Src} during mitosis \cite{stoverCdc2mediatedModulationPp60csrc1994}.
{\color{NavyBlue} This node represents high levels of \textit{Src} signaling under hypoxic conditions \cite{daiCSrcRequiredHypoxiainduced2019}.}

\textit{Nectins} form weak adhesions between adjacent cells by binding to \textit{Nectins} on other cells and promoting local membrane ruffling that is required for adherens junction formation \cite{takaiNectinsNectinlikeMolecules2003}. As downstream effects of \textit{Nectin3} - \textit{Nectin} binding between two cells do not require tight junction formation and high cell density, \textit{Nectin3} activation in our model only requires the presence of some neighbors.

{\textit{Necl-5} activity is controlled by co-localization with focal adhesions where it binds \textit{Spry2} and aids receptor tyrosine kinase signaling \cite{ogitaCellAdhesionMolecules2010}. We modeled this by turning the \textit{Necl-5} node ON when the \textit{Focal Adhesions} node is ON (indicating strong attachments that pull on the ECM and can form stress fibers), or in the absence of cell-cell adhesions at all sites of cell ECM-adhesion (i.e, fully surrounded with no free edge).}
\textit{SPRY2} (\textit{Sprouty 2}) is a negative regulator of growth factor-induced signaling, especially \textit{Ras/MAPK} \cite{kajitaRegulationPlateletderivedGrowth2007}.

\textit{E-cadherin} proteins are adhesion molecules required for adherens junction formation. The presence of juncitonal \textit{E-cadherin} (J\_Ecadherin = ON) in our model requires \textit{E-cadherin} mRNA expression, \textit{Nectin3}-mediated sensing of contact with neighboring cells (binding to nectins) \cite{ogitaCellAdhesionMolecules2010} and inactive Caspase 3 \cite{steinhusenCleavageSheddingEcadherin2001}.

Junctional \textit{E-cadherin} proteins binds to and recruits/sequesters \textit{$\beta$-catenin} to adherens junctions. This negatively regulates {$\beta$-catenin} mediated transcription, but aids adherens junction formation \cite{tianECadherinCateninComplex2011}. Here we assume that \textit{$\beta$-catenin} is localized to cell-cell junctions (\textit{J\_bcatenin} = ON) as long as there are \textit{E-cadherin}-mediated attachments to neighboring cells (even if a cell is not fully surrounded) and \textit{Caspase 3} is inactive \cite{steinhusenApoptosisinducedCleavageVCatenin2000}.

Junctional \textit{$\beta$-catenin} binds to and recruitcs \textit{$\alpha$-catenin} to adherens junctions. \textit{$\alpha$-catenin} links \textit{$\beta$-catenin} to the actin cytoskeleton to stabilize adherens junctions \cite{tianECadherinCateninComplex2011}.

\textit{Focal adhesions} form at sites of \textit{Integrin-ECM} attachment and clustering \cite{geigerEnvironmentalSensingFocal2009}. In order to take into account the effect of stiff ECM \cite{plotnikovForceFluctuationsFocal2012} as well as positive feedback between focal adhesion formation and horizontal cell polarization that creates an active leading edge, here we assume that force-generating Focal Adhesion formation requires ECM-Integrin attachments and \textit{FAK} \cite{kleinschmidtFocalAdhesionKinase2017}, and either strong traction force generation supported by a stiff ECM, or the existence of a leading edge with active \textit{Rac1} \cite{pasaperaRac1DependentPFocal2015} and \textit{IQGAP1} \cite{kozlovaIQGAP1RegulatesHyaluronanmediated2012,kohnoIQGAP1LinksPDGF2013,foroutannejadNovelRoleIQGAP12014} supported by \textit{YAP}-mediated upregulation of adhesion and focal adhesion-associated proteins \cite{nardoneYAPRegulatesCell2017}.

In order to model the independent effects of cell density and matrix stiffness on stress fiber formation, we assume that they require both the absence of high cell density, and the presence of focal adhesions attached to a stiff ECM.

YAP is a mechanosensitive transcriptional regulator of proliferation and migration, and its activation is controlled by both the cell’s ability to spread on an ECM (\textit{FocalAdhesions} and \textit{Stress\_Fibers}), and the lack of apical-basal polarity with mature adherens junctions that can sequester \textit{YAP} in the cytoplasm by binding and inhibitory phosphorylation. Experimental evidence indicates that in cells that maintain apical-basal polarity, several junctional proteins (\textit{$\alpha$-catenin}, \textit{AMOT}, \textit{Merlin}) and inhibitory kinases (\textit{Lats1} and \textit{Lats2} work together to sequester and block \textit{YAP} \cite{karamanCellJunctionsHippo2018,hoaCharacterisationLATS2Kinase2016}.
\textit{TRIO} is a \textit{Rac1}-activating GTP-exchange factor induced by \textit{YAP} \cite{parkSwitchlikeEnhancementEpithelialmesenchymal2019,shahYAPControlsCell2019}.

The Wilms Tumor 1 (\textit{WT1}) transcription factor is a repressor of \textit{E-cadherin} expression \cite{parkSwitchlikeEnhancementEpithelialmesenchymal2019}. Its nuclear localization is controlled by \textit{YAP} binding \cite{shahYAPControlsCell2019}.

\textit{TAZ} is a mechanosensitive transcriptional regulator of cell migration, and its activation is controlled by both the cell’s ability to spread on stiff ECM (\textit{Stress\_Fibers} = ON) and the lack of apical-basal polarity with mature adherens junctions that can sequestered \textit{TAZ} in the cytoplasm by binding and inhibitory phosphorylation \cite{dupontRoleYAPTAZ2011,parkSwitchlikeEnhancementEpithelialmesenchymal2019}. In cells that maintain apical-basal polarity, junctional proteins (\textit{$\alpha$-catenin}, \textit{AMOT}, \textit{Merlin}) and inhibitory kinases (\textit{Lats1} and \textit{Lats2}) work together to sequester and block \textit{TAZ} \cite{silvisAcateninTumorSuppressor2011,schlegelmilchYap1ActsDownstream2011,sarpalRoleACateninIts2019,dasguptaControlCellularResponses2019,hoaCharacterisationLATS2Kinase2016}.

Experiments show that \textit{YAP} and \textit{WT1} suppress but do not abolish \textit{E-cadherin} protein expression in areas of lowered cell density \cite{parkSwitchlikeEnhancementEpithelialmesenchymal2019}. To model this, we introduced a \textit{Ecadherin\_mRNA\_H} node that is blocked by \textit{YAP/WT1} repressor complexes (requiring their joint nuclear localization). \textit{Ecadherin\_mRNA\_H}, in turn, must be ON to allow cells to establish a ring of adherens junctions sufficient for apical-basal polarity.

In addition to a need for high cell density and cell-cell adhesion proteins that help assemble adherens junctions (\textit{Nectin3}, \textit{J\_Ecadherin}, \textit{J\_bcatenin}, \textit{J\_acatenin}), we assumed that either high (unimpeded) \textit{E-cadherin} mRNA expression or lack of a horizontally polarized cell morphology are required for the establishment of apical-basal polarity.

In cells that establish apical-basal cell polarity, \textit{Mst1} and \textit{2} activate the Hippo pathway by phosphorylating \textit{Lats1/2} kinases to promote \textit{YAP/TAZ} inhibition \cite{chanSte20likeKinaseMst22005,praskovaMOBKL1AMOBKL1BPhosphorylation2008,kwanDLG5ConnectsCell2016}.
\textit{Mst1/2} activate \textit{Lats1/2} kinases by phosphorylation, aided by their mutual binding to \textit{Merlin}.

In our model, \textit{AMOT} = ON represents phosphorylated and tight junction localized \textit{AMOT}, which requires \textit{Merlin} binding and \textit{Lats1/2} mediated phosphorylation \cite{hirateRoleAngiomotinPhosphorylation2014,yiTightJunctionassociatedMerlinangiomotin2011}.
\textit{YAP} induces the expression of microRNA \textit{miR-29c} to target \textit{PTEN} for degradation \cite{tumanengYAPMediatesCrosstalk2012}.

Cellular \textit{PTEN} is a tumor supressor phosphatase that reverses PIP2 $\rightarrow$ PIP3 conversion carried out by \textit{PI3K}, and thus supresses \textit{PI3K / AKT} signaling \cite{chenPTENTumorSuppressor2018}. The combinatorial effect of the distinct \textit{PTEN} regulators included below is not well documented. We chose to model cytoplasmic \textit{PTEN} availability as ON in the absence of \textit{miR-29c} \cite{tumanengYAPMediatesCrosstalk2012}. In addition, we combined the positive and negative effects of \textit{S6K}, \textit{ERK} and \textit{GSK3} by assuming that \textit{PTEN} is blocked by the joint action of \textit{ERK} and \textit{GSK3} in the presence of \textit{S6K}, and by either inhibitor in its absence.

\textit{Merlin} is functionally localized and able to mediate Hippo signaling when recruited by junctional $\beta$- and $\alpha$-\textit{catenin}, and not phosphorylated by high \textit{AKT1} {or the cooperative action of \textit{PAK1} and \textit{ILK}}. Since the \textit{AKT\_B} node in our model represents basal \textit{AKT} activity which co-occurs with \textit{Merlin}-mediated contact inhibition, we choose the peak \textit{AKT\_H} node to mark the level of \textit{AKT} signaling required to block \textit{Merlin}.

In our model, \textit{IQGAP1\_LeadingE} = ON represents \textit{IQGAP1} localized near the leading edge of a horizontally polarized cell, where it links focal adhesion-mediated and \textit{RTK}-mediated signaling \cite{kohnoIQGAP1LinksPDGF2013}. Its recruitment is sustained by well-established horizontal polarity, or induced by \textit{Rac1} \cite{fukataRolesRhofamilyGTPases2003} or \textit{RTK-Grb2} binding \cite{mcnultyMAPKScaffoldIQGAP12011,bensenorIQGAP1RegulatesCell2007,blagoevProteomicsStrategyElucidate2003}.

For cells to establish and maintain horizontal polarization, our model requires the lack of apical-basal polarization, the presence of an ECM, as well as asymmetric IQGAP1 localization \cite{watanabeRolesIQGAP1Cell2005}, focal adhesions and spreading (FAK \cite{watanabeRolesIQGAP1Cell2005,francoControlInitialEndothelial2011} and TAZ \cite{nardoneYAPRegulatesCell2017}).

Full \textit{Rac1} activation in our model requires the absence of \textit{caspase 3}, as well as horizontal polarization on a stiff ECM, Focal Adhesion formation, \textit{Necl-5} leading edge localization, \textit{TRIO} expression {\color{NavyBlue} and at least basal \textit{AKT} activity}. In addition, on soft ECM \textit{Rac1} activity is inhibited by the presence of \textit{miR-200} \cite{tangMicroRNA200bC3pRegulate2020} and \textit{miR-34} \cite{ahnZEB1DrivesPrometastatic2012}, as well as the cooperative action of \textit{Merlin}, \textit{Nectin3} and \textit{E-cadherin} at adherens and tight junctions \cite{kittRapidSuppressionActivated2011,yiTightJunctionassociatedMerlinangiomotin2011}.

{\color{NavyBlue} Full \textit{Rac1} activation in our model requires the absence of \textit{caspase 3}, as well as horizontal polarization on a stiff ECM, Focal Adhesion formation, \textit{Necl-5} leading edge localization and \textit{TRIO} expression. In addition, high \textit{Rac1} activity is inhibited by the presence of \textit{miR-200b/c} \cite{tangMicroRNA200bC3pRegulate2020}, \textit{miR-34} \cite{ahnZEB1DrivesPrometastatic2012}, as well as the cooperative action of \textit{Merlin}, \textit{Nectin3} and \textit{E-cadherin} at adherens and tight junctions \cite{kittRapidSuppressionActivated2011,yiTightJunctionassociatedMerlinangiomotin2011}. Finally, we assume that high \textit{Rac1} activity requires a stiff ECM \cite{baeFAKCasRacLamellipodinSignalingModule2014} and peak \textit{AKT} signaling.}

The \textit{p21}-Activated kinase 1 \textit{PAK1}, a serine-threonine kinase interacts with the Rho GTPases \textit{RAC1} and \textit{CDC42} to drive migration, survival, cell cycle, EMT, stress response and inflammation \cite{yaoP21ActivatedKinaseEmerging2020}. It is activated by \textit{Rac1}, which binds to \textit{PAK1} and stimulates its kinase activity \cite{knausStructuralRequirementsPAK1998}.

{\color{NavyBlue} In the current model, the \textit{Migration} node represents migration by a polarized cell, whereas \textit{Fast\_Migration} tracks rapid mesenchymal migration typical of a cell that underwent EMT. \textit{Migration} requires horizontal polarization, stress fiber maintenance, focal adhesion formation and the activity of {\color{NavyBlue}\textit{Rac1}} and \textit{PAK1} kinases \cite{depascalisSingleCollectiveCell2017,bokochBiologyP21ActivatedKinases2003}.}

In our model, the \textit{Fast\_Migration} node represents sustained mesenchymal migration of a polarized cell. This requires horizontal polarization, stress fiber maintenance, focal adhesion formation, high \textit{Rac1} actibity, as well as \textit{PAK1} kinase \cite{depascalisSingleCollectiveCell2017,bokochBiologyP21ActivatedKinases2003}.

{\color{NavyBlue}\textit{IKK$\alpha$} and \textit{IKK$\beta$} are two catalytic subunits of the \textit{IKK} protein complex}, composed of \textit{IKK$\alpha$} and \textit{IKK$\beta$}, and the regulatory protein \textit{NEMO}. Activation of the transcription factor \textit{NF-$\kappa$B} is mediated by the IKK complex, which phosphorylates and degrades the inhibitory \textit{I$\kappa$B} proteins \cite{mitchellSignalingNFkBSystem2016}.

\textit{NF-$\kappa$B} is a transcription factor primarily known as a master regulator of inflammatory signaling and the immune system. Its role in cancer is partly due to its ability to aid EMT. It is activated via the destruction of its inhibitory binding partner \textit{I$\kappa$B}, which is phosphorylated by the \textit{IKK} complex subsequently destroted \cite{mitchellSignalingNFkBSystem2016}.

\textit{c-Myb} is a transcription factor that can induce the epithelial micro-RNA \textit{miR-200} \cite{pieraccioliActivationMiR200CMyb2013}. \textit{c-Myb} is induced by \textit{AKT}-mediated activation of \textit{NF-$\kappa$B} and/or \textit{E2F1} \cite{lauderCMybTranscriptionActivated2001}.

{\textit{MCRIP1} is a binding partner and repressor of \textit{CtBP}, a binding partner of \textit{Zeb1} during transcription , and thus \textit{MCRIP1} blocks \textit{Zeb1}-mediated repression of \textit{E-cadherin} unless inhibited by \textit{ERK} phosphorylation \cite{ichikawaMCRIP1ERKSubstrate2015}.}
When released from cell-cell junctions, \textit{$\beta$-catenin} localizes to the nucleus and induces genes that promote proliferation and EMT \cite{bienzVCateninPivotCell2005}.

{The \textit{TGFb\_ext} node in our model represents an extracellular environment with saturating levels of \textit{TGF-$\beta$}. This input node is self-sustaining in the absence of \textit{in silico} perturbation.}

{The \textit{Self\_Loop} input node qualtifies the extent to which \textit{TGF-$\beta$} secreted by a single isolated cell can drive its own autocrine signaling to saturating levels. When tuned stochastically between 0 and 1, its level represents the fraction of saturating \textit{TGF-$\beta$} signal driven by the autocrine loop. We expect the fraction that accurately characterises a given cell to be a funciton of both cell type (intrinsic ability to secrete \textit{TGF-$\beta$}) and microenvironment, as the latter can influence diffusion and bio-availability of the secreted ligand.}

{The ON state of the \textit{TGF\_bRII} node represents a \textit{TGF-$\beta$}-bound \textit{T$\beta$RII} receptor, and thus requires external \textit{TGF-$\beta$} \cite{seoaneTGFvFamilySignaling2017}, or secreted \textit{TGF-$\beta$} along with either strong autocrine signaling (\textit{Self\_Loop}=ON) or at least medium cell density (\textit{CellDensity\_Low}=ON).}

{The ON state of \textit{T$\beta$RI} represents an active, ligand-bound receptor complex of \textit{TGF-$\beta$}, \textit{T$\beta$RII}, and \textit{T$\beta$RI} \cite{seoaneTGFvFamilySignaling2017}. Thus it requires \textit{TGF-$\beta$}-bound \textit{T$\beta$RII}, where \textit{TGF-$\beta$} is either externally supplied or secreted \textit{TGF-$\beta$} (the latter requiring strong autocrine signaling or medium cell density). }

{The \textit{SMAD2\_3\_4} node represents transcriptionally active \textit{Smad2/Smad3/Smad4} complexes. \textit{Smad2} and \textit{Smad3} are activated via phosphorylation by \textit{T$\beta$RI}, which releases them from the receptor complex to aid their nuclear translocation in partnership with \textit{Smad4} \cite{seoaneTGFvFamilySignaling2017}. \textit{SPRY2} reduces \textit{Smad} phosphorylation in dense monolayers \cite{tanSprouty2SuppressesEpithelialMesenchymal2016}, which also sequester \textit{TGF-$\beta$} receptors to their baso-lateral surface, hiding them from apically applied \textit{TGF-$\beta$} \cite{nallet-staubCellDensitySensing2015}. In contrast, \textit{YAP} and \textit{TAZ} bind to \textit{Smads}, aid their nuclear localization, and potentiate \textit{Smad}-induced transcription \cite{szetoYAPTAZAre2016}. Our model assumes that in order to respond to \textit{TGF-$\beta$}, cells either need active \textit{YAP/TAZ}, or no apical-basal polarizaiton.}

{\textit{HMGA2} is a transcription factor induced by \textit{SMAD 3/4} in response to \textit{TGF-$\beta$}. Once induced, it drives transcription of the master EMT switch by inducing \textit{SNAI1/2} and \textit{Twist} \cite{thuaultTransformingGrowthFactorbeta2006}.}

{\textit{TGF$\beta$-1} induces expression of the \textit{mTORC2} component \textit{Rictor}, \textit{ILK} binding to \textit{Rictor}, and \textit{ILK}-dependent \textit{Rictor} phosphorylation \cite{serranoRoleIntegrinlinkedKinase2013}. The complex, in turn, is known to activate \textit{AKT1} \cite{mcdonaldRictorIntegrinlinkedKinase2008}.}

{\textit{p15} (\textit{Ink4B}) is a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor that binds \textit{cdk4 / cdk6}, displacing \textit{Cyclin D} and thus blocking G1/S progression \cite{hannonP15INK4BPotentialEffector1994}. \textit{TGF$\beta$} induces both transcription \cite{fengSmad2Smad3Smad42000} and stabilization of \textit{p15} \cite{sandhuTransformingGrowthFactor1997}, while \textit{Myc} represses its transcription \cite{stallerRepressionP15INK4bExpression2001}. In addition, \textit{FoxO1/3} can also induce \textit{p15} \cite{katayamaFOXOTranscriptionFactordependent2008}.}

{\textit{TGF$\beta$} induces the transcription of the mitogen-activated protein kinase phosphatase \textit{MKP2}, or \textit{DUSP4}, through a \textit{SMAD3}-dependent mechanism \cite{rameshTGFvMediatedBIM2008}. \textit{DUSP4}, in turn, attenuates \textit{ERK} and allows \textit{BIM} accumulation, aiding \textit{TGF$\beta$}-mediated apoptosis \cite{rameshTGFvMediatedBIM2008,wildeySmad3PotentiatesTransforming2003}.}

{The \textit{Runx1} transcription factor is transcriptionally induced by \textit{TGF$\beta$}, leading to elevated mRNA and protein levels \cite{wildeyRunx1CoactivatorFOXO32009}. \textit{Runx1} in turns binds to \textit{FoxO3} to induce \textit{BIM} and promote \textit{TGF$\beta$}-mediated apoptosis \cite{wildeyRunx1CoactivatorFOXO32009}.}

\textit{SNAI1}, also known as \textit{Snail}, is a master inducer of EMT, responsible for starting the transcriptional cascade that locks in the EMT regulatory switch \cite{tianCoupledReversibleIrreversible2013}. In epithelial cells \textit{SNAI1} is repressed by RNA interference by \textit{miR-34} \cite{siemensMiR34SNAILForm2011} and protein degradation by \textit{GSK3} \cite{zhengGlycogenSynthaseKinase32013}. Transcription by \textit{NF-$\kappa$B} \cite{minNFkBEpithelialMesenchymal2008}, along with loss of repression by \textit{GSK3} and nuclear localization by \textit{PAK1} \cite{yangPak1PhosphorylationSnail2005}, can activate \textit{SNAI1}, starting EMT. In committed mesenhymal or hybrid E/M cells \textit{ZEB1} {\color{NavyBlue} and/or \textit{Hif-1$\alpha$}/\textit{$\beta$-catenin}\cite{xuSnailDirectTarget2015,xiIdentificationPY654vcateninCritical2013}} lower the barrier to maitnaining high levels of \textit{SNAI1}. Downstream of \textit{TGF}$\beta$, \textit{HMGA2} further aids its transcriptiopnal upregulation \cite{thuaultHMGA2SmadsCoregulate2008}{\color{NavyBlue}, as does\textit{HMGA1} \cite{zhongAssociationS100A13HMGA12016}.}

Lymphoid enhancer-binding factor 1, or \textit{LEF1} is a high-mobility group transcription factor and mediator of \textit{Wnt/$\beta$-catenin} signaling. In addition to promotong proliferation, \textit{LEF1} helps induce EMT by activating the transcription \textit{SNAI2} and \textit{ZEB1} \cite{santiagoWntSignalingPathway2017}. It is induced by \textit{NF-$\kappa$B} \cite{yunNFkBRegulatesLef12007} {or \textit{Smad2/4} \cite{nawshadTGFbeta3SignalingActivates2003}}, its transcriptional potency is boosted by \textit{ZEB1} \cite{rosmaninhoZeb1PotentiatesGenome2018}, and it is targeted for degradation by \textit{miR-200}.

\textit{SNAI2}, also known as \textit{Slug}, is a prototypical EMT transcription factor that regulates tissue development and tumorigenesis \cite{zhouMolecularRegulationSnai22019}. It is induced / maintained in mesenhymal cells by \textit{Twist} \cite{casasSnail2EssentialMediator2011}, \textit{$\beta$-catenin} \cite{saegusaRequirementAktBetacatenin2009,zhouMolecularRegulationSnai22019}, \textit{LEF1} \cite{lambertiniSLUGNewTarget2010} as well as positive auto-regulation \cite{kumarAutoregulationSlugMediates2015}. In response to \textit{TGF$\beta$} it is induced by \textit{Smad3} \cite{moritaDualRolesMyocardinrelated2007} and \textit{HMGA1/2} \cite{gandhiBimodalFunctionChromatin2020,thuaultTransformingGrowthFactorbeta2006}.

\textit{Twist} is a master trancriptional regulator of the EMT program, induced by \textit{NF-$\kappa$B} \cite{phamUpregulationTwist1NFkB2007} or \textit{HMGA2} \cite{tanRegulationTranscriptionFactor2012}, stabilized and aided by \textit{SNAI1}, repressed by \textit{miR-34} unless induced by \textit{YAP}, and cleaved during apoptosis by \textit{Caspase 3} \cite{demontisTwistSubstrateCaspase2006}. {\color{NavyBlue} Under hypoxia, \textit{Twist} is induced by complex formation between \textit{Src}-phosphorylated \textit{$\beta$-catenin} and \textit{Hif-1$\alpha$} \cite{xiIdentificationPY654vcateninCritical2013}.}

\textit{miR-34} is an microRNA expressed in epithelial cells and central to blocking the accumulation of EMT-initiating transcription factors such as \textit{SNAI1} and \textit{$\beta$-catenin} \cite{zhangMicroRNA34FamilyPotential2019}. \textit{SNAI1}, together with \textit{ZEB1}, feed back to repress \textit{miR-34} expression in mesenhymal and hybrid E/M cells \cite{nieRolesMicroRNA34aEpithelial2019}.

The \textit{miR-200b} microRNA is expressed in epithelial cells and is central to blocking EMT transcription factors \cite{mongrooRoleMiR200Family2010}. {\color{NavyBlue} Its levels are increased by \textit{p21} \cite{liP21ZEB1ComplexInhibits2014},} and it is directly induced by \textit{c-Myb} \cite{pieraccioliActivationMiR200CMyb2013} and repressed by \textit{ZEB1} \cite{burkReciprocalRepressionZEB12008,haraguchiDynamicsPlasticityEpithelial2016}. This repression is indirectly supported by \textit{SNAI1} \cite{gillSnailMicroRNA200Family2011,moesNovelNetworkIntegrating2012} and \textit{Twist} \cite{daveFunctionalCooperationSnail12011}. Here we assume that in addition to the absence of \textit{p21} and the aid of \textit{SNAI1} and \textit{Twist}, {\color{NavyBlue} either \textit{ZEB2} or} high levels of \textit{ZEB1} (\textit{ZEB\_H} = ON) are required to silence the active \textit{miR-200} promoter. In contrast, medium \textit{ZEB1} can maintain repression as long as \textit{miR-200} inducer \textit{c-Myb} is off.

The \textit{miR-200c} microRNA is expressed in epithelial cells and is central to blocking EMT transcription factors \cite{mongrooRoleMiR200Family2010}. It is directly induced by \textit{c-Myb} \cite{pieraccioliActivationMiR200CMyb2013} and repressed by \textit{ZEB1} {\color{NavyBlue}or \textit{ZEB2} \cite{burkReciprocalRepressionZEB12008,haraguchiDynamicsPlasticityEpithelial2016,burkReciprocalRepressionZEB12008,haraguchiDynamicsPlasticityEpithelial2016,brackenDoubleNegativeFeedbackLoop2008}}. This repression is indirectly supported by \textit{SNAI1} \cite{gillSnailMicroRNA200Family2011,moesNovelNetworkIntegrating2012} and \textit{Twist} \cite{daveFunctionalCooperationSnail12011}. Here we assume that in addition to the aid of \textit{SNAI1} and \textit{Twist}, high levels of \textit{ZEB1} (\textit{ZEB\_H} = ON) {\color{NavyBlue}or \textit{ZEB2}} are required to silence the active \textit{miR-200} promoter. In contrast, medium \textit{ZEB1} can maintain repression as long as \textit{miR-200} is silenced and its inducer \textit{c-Myb} is off.

The \textit{ZEB1\_H} node represents maximal \textit{ZEB1} activation seen in fully mesenchymal cells \cite{jollyImplicationsHybridEpithelial2015, luMicroRNAbasedRegulationEpithelialhybridmesenchymal2013,zhangTGFvinducedEpithelialtomesenchymalTransition2014}. In our model this requires medium \textit{ZEB1}, as well as \textit{LEF1} \cite{kobayashiTranscriptionFactorLEF12013}, either \textit{SNAI2} \cite{welsTranscriptionalActivationZEB12011} or the absence of \textit{miR-200} \cite{liMiR200CanRepress2014,titleGeneticDissectionMiR200Zeb12018}, as well as either high nuclear \textit{$\beta$-catenin} \cite{sanchez-tilloVcateninTCF4Complex2011}{\color{NavyBlue} high \textit{Hif-1$\alpha$}\cite{zhangHIF1aPromotesEpithelialMesenchymal2015}, \textit{$\beta$-catenin/TCF4}\cite{sanchez-tilloVcateninTCF4Complex2011}, or \textit{HMGA1}\cite{aiHMGA1AggravatesOxidative2023}.}

Zinc finger E-box binding homeobox 1 or \textit{ZEB1} is one of the core regulators of the EMT transcriptional switch \cite{drapelaZEB1CriticalRegulator2020}. It is induced by \textit{SNAI2} \cite{welsTranscriptionalActivationZEB12011}, nuclear \textit{$\beta$-catenin/TCF4} \cite{sanchez-tilloVcateninTCF4Complex2011}, {\color{NavyBlue}\textit{Twist} aided by \textit{SMAD2/3/4}, or high levels of \textit{Hif-1$\alpha$}.} The epithelial microRNA \textit{miR-200} targets its mRNA for destruction \cite{liMiR200CanRepress2014,titleGeneticDissectionMiR200Zeb12018}. As \textit{ZEB1} has two distinct activation levels in hybrid E/M cells vs fully mesenchynmal ones \cite{jollyImplicationsHybridEpithelial2015, luMicroRNAbasedRegulationEpithelialhybridmesenchymal2013,zhangTGFvinducedEpithelialtomesenchymalTransition2014}, we modeled \textit{ZEB1} activity with two nodes; this one represents at least medium \textit{ZEB1} activity (characteristic of hybrid E/M cells and compatible with ongoing \textit{miR-200} expression), and the \textit{ZEB1\_H} node representing maximal \textit{ZEB1} activation seen in fully mesenchymal cells.

{\color{NavyBlue} Zinc finger E-box binding homeobox 2 or \textit{ZEB2} is a core regulator of the EMT transcriptional switch. \textit{ZEB2} is transcriptionally induced by either \textit{NF-$\kappa$B} aided by moderate \textit{Hif-1$\alpha$}, \textit{SMAD2/3/4} \cite{katohIntegrativeGenomicAnalyses2009}, or high levels of \textit{Hif-1$\alpha$}. It is blocked by \textit{miR\_200c}-mediated mRNA degradation \cite{parkMiR200FamilyDetermines2008}.}

{\color{NavyBlue} \textit{HMGA1} is a high mobility group (HMG) proteininvolved in transcriptional regulation via chromatin remodeling. It is directly induced by \textit{$\beta$-catenin/TCF-4}-mediated transcription \cite{bushWntVcateninTcell2013}, and indirectly stabilized by \textit{ZEB2} repression of the the \textit{miR-637} mRNA (which targets its mRNA for degradation) \cite{zengOncogenicZEB2MiR6372021}.}

The \textit{N\_bcatenin\_H} node represents maximal nuclear \textit{$\beta$-catenin} accumulation. This requires \textit{N\_bcatenin} = ON, a lack of \textit{miR-34}, either complete absence of junctions (\textit{J\_acatenin} = OFF) {or activation by \textit{Smads}}, and the lack of joint repression \textit{GSK3} and either \textit{miR-200} or \textit{CyclinE/A}-bound \textit{Cdk2}.

{\color{NavyBlue} The \textit{$\beta$-catenin-Hif-1$\alpha$} node represents complexes formed by nuclear \textit{$\beta$-catenin} and \textit{Hif-1$\alpha$} under hypoxic conditions, promoting transcription of mesenchymal-associated genes \cite{xiIdentificationPY654vcateninCritical2013}. This complex formation is aided by high levels of active \textit{Src} and a hypoxic increase in ROS\cite{xiIdentificationPY654vcateninCritical2013}.}

The \textit{Ecadherin\_mRNA} represents basal \textit{E-cadherin} expression, required to make at least some adherens juncitons with neighbors. This basal expression is only blocked during full EMT by the joint action of \textit{ZEB1} \cite{shirakiharaDifferentialRegulationEpithelial2007}, \textit{SNAI1} \cite{bolosTranscriptionFactorSlug2003,parkMiR200FamilyDetermines2008,nieRolesMicroRNA34aEpithelial2019}, \textit{SNAI2} \cite{bolosTranscriptionFactorSlug2003,peinadoTranscriptionalRegulationCadherins2004,parkMiR200FamilyDetermines2008}, \textit{Twist} \cite{vesunaTwistTranscriptionalRepressor2008,nieRolesMicroRNA34aEpithelial2019}, {\color{NavyBlue} and\textit{ZEB2}}; protected from repression by \textit{MCRIP1} \cite{wengMCRIP1PromotesExpression2019}.

The \textit{b\_catenin\_TCF4} node represents saturating levels of active nuclear \textit{$\beta$-catenin/TCF4} transcriptional activity. In addition to the influences required to accumulate high nuclear \textit{$\beta$-catenin}, this node's ON state also requires \textit{SNAI1} and \textit{SNAI2} expression (both factors promote the formation of active \textit{$\beta$-catenin/TCF4} transcriptional complexes) \cite{mediciSnailSlugPromote2008} and low \textit{miR-200c} levels. {\color{NavyBlue}High levels of \textit{Hif-1$\alpha$}, aided by ROS, sequester \textit{$\beta$-catenin} away from \textit{TCF4} \cite{bouazizInteractionHIF1aVcatenin2016}.}

The \textit{TGFb\_secr} node represents the production and secretion of \textit{TGF$\beta$} by the modeled cell. \textit{TGF$\beta$} transcription in mesenchymal cells is driven by nuclear \textit{$\beta$-catenin/TCF4}-mediated transcription, while \textit{TGF$\beta$} mRNA is targeted for degradation by \textit{miR-200} \cite{gregoryAutocrineTGFbetaZEB2011}. {\color{NavyBlue}Alternately, hypoxia or loss of \textit{VHL} protein allows \textit{Hif-1$\alpha$} to increase \textit{TGF$\beta$} secretion\cite{mcmahonHypoxiaenhancedExpressionProprotein2005,pengHypoxiaInducibleFactor1a2018}. Finally, apoptotic \textit{Caspase 3} disrupts all ER-mediated protein secretion\cite{loweCaspasemediatedCleavageSyntaxin2004}.}

{\color{NavyBlue} The \textit{Hypoxia} input node represents an environment with less than 1\% cellular oxygen level, or $CoCl_2$ treatment mimicking hypoxia. \cite{semenzaDefiningRoleHypoxiaInducible2010}.}

{\color{NavyBlue} This node represents basal expression of \textit{Hif-1$\alpha$}, observed under normoxic conditions in dividing cells, part of the Warburg effect (aerobic glycolysis) \cite{courtnayCancerMetabolismWarburg2015}. It plays a similar role to the \textit{HIF1} node in our previosly published model of mitochodrial dysfunction-induced senescence \cite{sizekUnlockingMitochondrialDysfunctionAssociated2023}.} {\color{PineGreen} Links in turquoise font are copied from this model.}

{\color{NavyBlue} This model uses \textit{Hif1a\_High} to indicate a strong but non-lethal level of \textit{Hif-1$\alpha$} accumulation, induced by hypoxia or complete knockdown of \textit{Hif-1$\alpha$} repressors.}
{\color{NavyBlue} ROS accumulation is associated with hypoxic conditions due to metabolic disruption in the mitochondria. \cite{guzyMitochondrialComplexIII2005}}

{\color{NavyBlue} Von Hippel Lindau protein is the primary subunit of a ubiquitin ligase responsible for recognizing \textit{Hif-1$\alpha$}, leading to its oxygen-dependent degredation \cite{marxsenHypoxiainducibleFactor1HIF12004}.}

{\color{NavyBlue} \textit{PHD1/2} are prolyl hydroxylases responsible for hydroxylating the oxygen-dependent degredation domain of \textit{Hif-1$\alpha$}, leading to ubiqitination by VHL protein under normoxic conditions. \textit{PHD1/2} require molecular oxygen for hydroxylation \cite{marxsenHypoxiainducibleFactor1HIF12004}.}

{\color{NavyBlue} miR-17-92 is a microRNA responsible for negatively regulating the hypoxic response pathway \cite{taguchiIdentificationHypoxiaInducibleFactor1a2008}. It is induced in dividing cells by \textit{Myc}.}

{\color{NavyBlue} Factor Inhibiting HIF1, of \textit{FIH}, is an asparaginyl hydroxylase that depends on Fe(II) and uses uses molecular O2 to modify its substrates. Under normoxia, it represses \textit{Hif-1$\alpha$} through inhibition of its transactivation domain \cite{mahonFIH1NovelProtein2001} by hydroxylation of asparagine residues that mediate recruitment of the p300 cofactor \cite{landoFIH1AsparaginylHydroxylase2002a}.}

In this model, the \textit{p21} node corresponds to nuclear p21 in cells with relatively high basal \textit{p21} activity. \textit{p21} activity and or localization can be lowered by loss of \textit{FoxO} mediated transcription (see \textit{p21\textsubscript{mRNA}} node), via feedback from \textit{Cyclin E/Cdk2} \cite{overtonBasalP21Controls2014}, {\color{NavyBlue} or repression by \textit{Myc}\cite{gartelMycRepressesP212001}}.

\textit{pRB} is active in the absence of \textit{Caspase 3}, \textit{Cyclin D1}, \textit{Cyclin A}, and \textit{Cyclin E}. In addition, \textit{pRB} maintains its activity when active \textit{p27\textsuperscript{Kip1}} counteracts the effects of \textit{Cyclin E} \cite{coqueretNewRolesP212003,harbourCdkPhosphorylationTriggers1999,NovakMammalianCellCycle2004,tayaRBKinasesRBbinding1997}.

Active \textit{p27}$^{Kip1}$ is cleaved by \textit{Caspase 3} and inhibited (sequestered) by \textit{Cyclin D1/Cdk4,6} \cite{coqueretNewRolesP212003} or \textit{Cyclin B/Cdk1} \cite{ishidaPhosphorylationP27Kip1Serine2002}. In addition, maintenance of \textit{p27}$^{Kip1}$ requires one or both \textit{FoxO} factors when sequestered by \textit{Cyclin E/Cdk2} (one \textit{FoxO} factor) or \textit{Cyclin A/Cdk2} (both \textit{FoxO} factors), but it cannot keep pace with the simultaneous activity of \textit{Cyclin E/Cdk2} and \textit{Cyclin A/Cdk2} \cite{faureDynamicalAnalysisGeneric2006}.

\textit{Myc} activity is turned on by stabilization of the protein via \textit{ERK} phosphorylation, aided by \textit{YAP}-mediated transcription \cite{chenCMYCBCL2Mediate2018,liInhibitionYAPSuppresses2016} in the absence of inhibitory \textit{SMADs} \cite{chenDefectiveRepressionCmyc2001}{\color{NavyBlue} and aided by \textit{TCF4/$\beta$-catenin}, the absence of inhibitory \textit{$/beta$-catenin-Hif-1$\alpha$} complexes}. To take into account the increase in translation initiated by \textit{eIF4E} and loss of degradation-promoting phosphorylation when \textit{GSK3$\beta$} is off \cite{searsMultipleRasdependentPhosphorylation2000}, we assumed that they can compensate for the lack of \textit{ERK}, absence of \textit{YAP}, {or interference from \textit{SMADs}}. Alternatively, increased transcription by \textit{E2F1} can also promote \textit{Myc} accumulation in the absence of active \textit{pRB} \cite{roussel1994dual}, provided that the protein is stabilized by \textit{ERK}, \textit{eIF4E}, or the absence of \textit{GSK3$\beta$}. {\color{NavyBlue} Lastly, high levels of \textit{Hif-1$\alpha$} repress \textit{Myc} activity\cite{koshijiHIF1aInducesCell2004}.}

Ongoing DNA synthesis keeps the \textit{CHK1} kinase active, which inhibits \textit{Cyclin D1}. {Similarly, the CDKI \textit{p15} also binds and blocks active \textit{Cdk/Cyclin D} complexes.} The precise regulatory logic of \textit{Cyclin D1} as a function of transcriptional control by \textit{Myc} and \textit{E2F1}, combined with the regulation of its protein stability / activity by \textit{GSK3$\beta$} / basal \textit{p21} is not known. Here, we assume that in the absence of \textit{p21} (once \textit{p21} levels drop due to growth factor signals and/or \textit{Cdk2} activation), \textit{Cyclin D1} can be activated by \textit{YAP} and either \textit{Myc} or \textit{E2F1} -- as long as \textit{GSK3$\beta$ is OFF}. In the presence of \textit{GSK3$\beta$}, we assume that \textit{Cyclin D1} can be induced by the combined action of both \textit{Myc} and \textit{E2F1} \cite{leungRoleMycFacilitating2008}, but sustained in an ON state by either. In the presence of basal (normal quiescent) levels of \textit{p21}, we assume that \textit{Cyclin D1} transcription requires \textit{E2F1} unencumbered by \textit{pRB}, as well as any two of the following: \textit{Myc}, already active \textit{Cyclin D1}, sustained by \textit{YAP} and not blocked by \textit{GSK3$\beta$}.

In the absence of both \textit{CyclinA} and \textit{pRB}, \textit{E2F1} transcription can be induced by \textit{YAP} and \textit{Myc} or maintained by active \textit{E2F1}. \textit{CAD} deactivates \textit{E2F1} as it destroys the cell’s DNA.

In our model, the ON state of \textit{Cyclin E} represents active \textit{Cyclin E/Cdk2} complexes. Thus, its full activation requires transcription via \textit{E2F1} not blocked by active \textit{pRB}, binding to \textit{Cdc6} and \textit{pre-RC} complexes, and the absence of its inhibitors \textit{p27\textsuperscript{Kip1}}, \textit{CHK1} and \textit{Caspase 3}. {\color{NavyBlue} In additon, we assume that moderate \textit{HIF-1$\alpha$} accumulation seen in G1 is required for the mitochodrial ATP boost that aids \textit{Cyclin E} activation and S-phase entry\cite{mitraHyperfusedMitochondrialState2009,sizekUnlockingMitochondrialDysfunctionAssociated2023}. Once active, we assume that \textit{CyclinE} can maintain its activity without the ongoing presence of \textit{HIF-1$\alpha$}.}

\textit{ORC} proteins can bind at origins of replication when transcribed by \textit{E2F1} or as part of a fully assembled and licensed \textit{Pre-RC} complex (including active \textit{Cdc6} and \textit{Cdt1}).

In our model the \textit{Cdc6} node represents nuclear, chromatin-bound \textit{Cdc6}. Thus, the node is only active during the assembly of pre-replication complexes, or their ongoing presence during DNA replication. \textit{Cdc6} is ON in the absence of \textit{Caspase 3} or \textit{CyclinA / Cdk2} phosphorylation of \textit{Cdc6} in all origins required for the completion of DNA replication (thus, its inhibition by \textit{Cyclin A} also requires 4N DNA). In addition, active \textit{Cdc6} requires either transcription by \textit{E2F1} and recruitment by origin-bound \textit{ORC} proteins in the absence of mitotic \textit{Plk1} or maintenance of \textit{Pre-RCs} by the presence of all of its components.

Replication-origin bound \textit{Cdt1} requires the absence of \textit{geminin}, the presence of origin-bound \textit{ORC} and \textit{Cdc6}, and the absence of sustained \textit{Cdk2} activity responsible for the firing of all origins during DNA synthesis (modeled as simultaneous \textit{Cyclin E}, \textit{Cyclin A} and \textit{Cdc25A} activity). Bound into a licensed pre-replication complex (\textit{Pre-RC}), \textit{Cdt1} remains stable as long as it is transcribed by \textit{E2F1} \cite{yoshidaRegulationGemininCdt12004} or \textit{Myc} \cite{valovkaTranscriptionalControlDNA2013} (this guarantees that \textit{Pre-RC} complexes cannot persist indefinitely in the absence of de novo transcription). Alternatively, it can be turned on by \textit{E2F1}, aided by \textit{Myc} or the absence of \textit{RB}, and \textit{FoxO3} in cells with 4N DNA.

\textit{Pre-RC} complexes assemble when \textit{ORC}, \textit{Cdc6}, and \textit{Cdt1} are all bound to sites of replication origin along the DNA. The node denoting their licensing turns OFF at the moment of transition from ongoing \textit{Replication} to \textit{f4N\_DNA} (it is blocked in the one time-point when both of these nodes are ON).

\textit{Geminin} is present when transcribed by \textit{E2F1} and not targeted for degradation by \textit{APC/C\textsuperscript{Cdh1}} or \textit{APC/C\textsuperscript{Cdc20}} \cite{Clijsters:2013do}.
In non-apoptotic cells (no \textit{CAD}), \textit{Cyclin A} is transcribed by \textit{E2F1} in the absence of active \textit{RB} or by \textit{FoxM1}.

Our model allows the sustained presence of \textit{Emi1} protein when it is either actively transcribed by \textit{E2F1} \cite{tateguTranscriptionalRegulationHuman2008,hsuE2FdependentAccumulationHEmi12002} or lacks joint inhibition by \textit{pRB} \cite{hsuE2FdependentAccumulationHEmi12002} and \textit{p21} \cite{leeDNADamageTriggers2009}. Degradation of \textit{Emi1} is mediated by \textit{Plk1} and \textit{CyclinB/Cdk1} complexes; initiation of this degradation requires at least temporary co-localization of \textit{Emi1} with \textit{Plk1} at mitotic spindle poles \cite{hansenPlk1RegulatesActivation2004}.

In our model, \textit{FoxM1} activity requires increased expression by \textit{Myc} \cite{panTranscriptionFactorFoxM12018} or \textit{YAP} \cite{mizunoYAPInducesMalignant2012} and activating phosphorylation by \textit{Cyclin E/Cdk2}. Alternatively, \textit{FoxM1} activity can be sustained by potent \textit{Cdk2 / Cdk1} activity in G2 (supported by \textit{Cdc25A} or \textit{Cdc25B}), or a serial phosphorylation by \textit{Cyclin B/Cdk1} and \textit{Plk1} during mitosis.

As the precise combinatorial regulation of \textit{Cdc25A} throughput the cell cycle is unknown, our model assumes that accumulation of the \textit{Cdc25A} protein requires transcriptional activation by both \textit{E2F1} in the absence of \textit{pRB}, and \textit{FoxM1} to override destruction by \textit{APC/C\textsuperscript{Cdh1}}. Alternatively, one of the two transcription factors can drive \textit{Cdc25A} accumulation in the absence of \textit{APC/C\textsuperscript{Cdh1}}. In addition, stabilization of \textit{Cdc25A} either requires the absence of \textit{GSK3$\beta$} and \textit{CHK1} (both of which promote its degradation), or stabilization by \textit{Cdk} activity.
\textit{Wee1} is active during \textit{Replication}, unless its activity is blocked by \textit{CyclinA/Cdk1} OR \textit{CyclinB/Cdk1} \cite{Deibler:2010ds}.
\textit{Cdc25B} activation requires transcription by \textit{FoxM1}, centrosomal localization, and activation by \textit{Aurora A} kinase on replicated centrosomes.

\textit{Plk1} activity requires the absence of \textit{APC/C\textsuperscript{Cdh1}}, transcription by \textit{FoxM1}, or high \textit{Plk1} levels transcribed earlier by both \textit{FoxM1} and \textit{FoxO3} (see \textit{Plk1\_H} below) \cite{alvarezForkheadTranscriptionFactors2001}. In addition, \textit{Plk1} activation requires phosphorylation by either \textit{CyclinB/Cdk1} during mitosis or \textit{Cyclin A/Cdk2} (aided by lack of \textit{Wee1} and \textit{Cdc25A}) at the G2/M boundary \cite{gheghianiPLK1ActivationLate2017}.

\textit{Cyclin A} activity requires transcription (\textit{Cyclin A} mRNA) and the absence of degradation by phosphorylated (mitotic) \textit{pAPC}. In addition, turning ON inactive \textit{Cyclin A} requires activation of \textit{Cdk2} by \textit{Cdc25A} \cite{blombergEctopicExpressionCdc25A1999} and the absence / \textit{Emi1}-mediated inhibition of \textit{APC/C\textsuperscript{Cdh1}}. Once active, \textit{Cyclin A} maintains its activity in the absence of overpowering influences driving its degradation. Namely, \textit{Cyclin A} relies on either \textit{Emi1} or the absence of \textit{UbcH10} for its ability to keep inactive \textit{APC/C\textsuperscript{Cdh1}} in check. To overpower active \textit{APC/C\textsuperscript{Cdh1}}, \textit{Cyclin A} requires both \textit{Emi1} and no \textit{UbcH10}. The precise combinatorial regulation of \textit{Cyclin A} is not known; the above logic is consistent with \textit{Cyclin A} activity pattern during cell cycle progression.

In our model, \textit{Cdc25C} is active in cells with replicated DNA (see \textit{f4N\_DNA} $\rightarrow$ \textit{Cdc25C} link). Its activation is initiated by a small, initially cytoplasmic pool of \textit{Cyclin B/Cdk1} activated by \textit{Cdc25B} (not directly represented in our model) and further increased by \textit{Cdc25B} itself, which translocates to the nucleus with the aid of \textit{Plk1}. During mitosis, \textit{Plk1} potentiates the ability of \textit{Cyclin B/Cdk1} to maintain \textit{Cdc25C} activity.

\textit{Cyclin B} node is ON when the concentration of \textit{Cyclin B} proteins is high (does not represent the activity of \textit{CyclinB/Cdk1} complexes). This occurs when \textit{Cyclin B} is transcribed by \textit{FoxM1}, maintained by \textit{FoxO3} transcription, and not undergoing \textit{APC}-mediated degradation by \textit{APC/C\textsuperscript{Cdc20}} or \textit{APC/C\textsuperscript{Cdh1}}.

The ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme (E2) \textit{UbcH10} is active in the absence of \textit{Cdh1}. Alternatively, active \textit{UbcH10} is maintained in the presence of \textit{Cdh1} when some of its targets are present: \textit{Cdc20} OR \textit{CyclinA} OR \textit{CyclinB} \cite{Rape:2004em}.

Full \textit{Cdk1} kinase activation requires its binding partner \textit{Cyclin B} and the \textit{Cdc25C} phosphatase, which maintains \textit{Cdk1} in an active dephosphorylated state. \textit{Cdk1} is inhibited by the checkpoint kinase \textit{CHK1}, unless it is already full active and \textit{Wee1} kinase is inhibited.

In line with evidence that \textit{Plk1} can aid full activation of \textit{APC/C}, but \textit{Cdk1} appears to be the more potent inducer, our model requires both \textit{Cyclin B/Cdk1} and \textit{Plk1} to activate \textit{APC/C} from an OFF state, but only \textit{Cdk1} activity to maintain it. In addition, ongoing phosphorylation of the functional \textit{APC/C\textsuperscript{Cdc20}} complex is no longer required.

In our model, \textit{APC/C\textsuperscript{Cdc20}} complex formation is represented by the joint activity of \textit{Cdc20} and phosphorylated \textit{APC/C} (\textit{pAPC}). \textit{Cdc20} is thus ON in the presence of \textit{pAPC} when both \textit{Emi1} and \textit{Cdh1} are absent (\textit{APC/C\textsuperscript{Cdh1}} is represented by the \textit{Cdh1} node, see below). In addition, \textit{Cdc20} activity requires either the absence of \textit{Mad2} at unattached kinetochores, or the absence of \textit{Cdc20} phosphorylation by \textit{Cyclin B/Cdk1} or by \textit{Cyclin A/Cdk2} complexes to potentiate the interaction between \textit{Mad2} and \textit{Cdc20}, and \textit{pAPC} is ON (present and phosphorylated) \cite{dangiolellaSpindleCheckpointRequires2003}.

\textit{APC/C\textsuperscript{Cdh1}} activity requires the absence of Cyclin Dependent kinase phosphorylation by \textit{Cyclin B/Cdk1}, or \textit{Cyclin A/Cdk2} aided by further inhibition of \textit{Cdh1} by \textit{Emi1}, or ongoing \textit{Cdk2} activation by \textit{Cdc25A} in the absence of \textit{Emi1}.

The \textit{Replication} node represents ongoing DNA synthesis. This requires a non-apoptotic cell, licensed pre-replication complexes (\textit{Pre\_RC}). The start of DNA synthesis requires \textit{E2F1}-meditated transcription of the genes that help execute it, as well as the firing of the first round of replication origins by \textit{Cyclin E/Cdk2}. Once ongoing, replication is sustained by \textit{Cyclin A/Cdk2} and \textit{Cdc25A}, aided by \textit{E2F1} and terminated by completion of a full round of synthesis (\textit{4N\_DNA}).
\textit{ATR} accumulates at replication forks during unperturbed DNA synthesis \cite{Petermann:2006fj}.

\textit{ATR} kinase activates \textit{CHK1} at replication forks, which not only blocks premature mitosis but also regulates the rate of origin firing by keeping \textit{Cdc25} protein levels from increasing above their physiological range \cite{Petermann:2006fj}.

4N DNA content in our model is reached via the completion of \textit{Replication} (via the firing of the last round of replication origins by \textit{Cyclin A/Cdk} complexes) and maintained in non-apoptotic cells the absence of a contractile ring driving cytokinesis.

Our model represents the SAC via the \textit{Mad2} kinetochore-binding protein. \textit{Mad2} is active as long as the cell has at least one unattached kinetochore and it is responsible for keeping \textit{Cdc20} sequestered from \textit{APC/C}. By keeping \textit{APC} at bay until the spindle is complete, \textit{Mad2} is required for the proper timing of anaphase \cite{Nezi:2009je}.

The \textit{U\_Kinetochores} node in our model is on from the moment the nuclear envelope is dissolved in prometaphase and the mitotic spindle starts to form, until all kinetochores are properly attached. In addition to the presence of unattached kinetochores, \textit{U\_Kinetochores} = ON requires attached sister chromatics, the absence of \textit{APC/C\textsuperscript{Cdh1}} activity. It is turned on my \textit{Cyclin B/Cdk1} and remains on until the spindle is complete (or it is destroyed by \textit{APC/C\textsuperscript{Cdh1}}).

The completed spindle, represented by the \textit{A\_Kinetochores} node, requires replicated and attached sister chromatids (\textit{f4N\_DNA}) and the absence of \textit{APC/C} activity. It turns on when the process of spindle assembly (\textit{U\_Kinetochores}) is completed by active \textit{Src}, active \textit{Plk1} localized to unattached kinetochores in the presence of ongoing \textit{Cyclin B/Cdk1} activity, and it remains on until anaphase (\textit{APC/C} activation).

The ON state of \textit{Plk1\_H} encodes the short-lived memory of a sufficiently large active \textit{Plk1} pool to temporarily survive \textit{Plk1} destruction by \textit{APC/C\textsuperscript{Cdh1}} \cite{Lindon:2004kl}, recruit \textit{Ect2} to the central spindle, and thus aid the completion of cytokinesis \cite{petronczkiPololikeKinaseTriggers2007}. Thus, \textit{Plk1\_H} requires ongoing \textit{Plk1} activation and transcription by \textit{FoxM1}, and either induction by \textit{FoxO3} or \textit{FoxO1}, or prior accumulation.

\textit{Ect2} activaiton at the spindle midzone represents the step of cytokinesis in our model. Thus, \textit{Ect2} requires \textit{f4N\_DNA}, high \textit{Plk1} activity, as well as \textit{Cdh1} for the assembly of a normal spindle midzone. Finally, \textit{Ect2} cannot be recruited to the mid zone before anaphase is completed.

In contrast to our previous model in \cite{sizekBooleanModelGrowth2019} where \textit{Ect2} recruitment to the central spindle marked the start of cytokinesis, in \cite{gubermanBooleanModelAnchorage2020} we introduced a separate \textit{Cytokinesis} node to mark cytokinesis and the subsequent resetting of daughter cell DNA content to 2N by a separate node. In addition to \textit{Ect2} recruitment, completion of cytokinesis also requires ECM attachments able to activate \textit{FAK} and \textit{Src} kinases.
The \textit{Trail} node represents environmental availability of the \textit{Trail} protein outside the cell.
The \textit{DR4} and \textit{DR5} death receptors, represented by the \textit{DR4\_5} node, are activated by extracellular \textit{Trail} \cite{Guicciardi:2009km}.
\textit{Pro-Caspase 8} may be cleaved independently by \textit{DISC} (not directly reprsented; an adaptor protein for \textit{DR4\_5}) or \textit{Caspase 3}.

\textit{Pro-caspase 2} is cleaved and activated by \textit{Caspase 3}, or by failed cytokinesis marked by the presence of unattached kinetochores, an active SAC, and the absence of active \textit{Cyclin B/Cdk1} complexes to phosphorylate and inhibit \textit{Caspase 2}.

\textit{Caspase 3} or \textit{2}-mediated destruction of \textit{MCL-1} must be absent for \textit{MCL-1} to be ON. Avoiding degradation via textit{GSK3} requires the \textit{GSK3}-weakenjng presence of basal \textit{AKT} activity (\textit{AKT\_B}) \cite{Maurer:2006bo} and either \textit{ERK}-mediated stabilization, or the absence of its repressor \textit{E2F1}. Finally, during mitotic arrest (\textit{U\_Kinetochores}), \textit{MCL-1} is deactivated by \textit{Cyclin B/Cdk1} phosphorylation, which shields it from the \textit{PPA2}-mediated dephosphorylation of its degradation-targeting sites \cite{wertzSensitivityAntitubulinChemotherapeutics2011}.

\textit{Bcl-x\textsubscript{L}} activity requires the absence of \textit{Caspase 3}. In addition, \textit{BAD} can block \textit{Bcl-x\textsubscript{L}}, as it preferentially binds to it rather than \textit{BCL2} (meaning in the absence of the latter \textit{Bcl-x\textsubscript{L}} is more likely to be sequestered by basal levels of \textit{BAD}) \cite{yangBadHeterodimericPartner1995}. {Similarly, \textit{TFG}$\beta$ can also repress \textit{Bcl-x\textsubscript{L}} \cite{spenderTGFbetaInducesApoptosis2009}.} Lastly, mitotic \textit{Bcl-x\textsubscript{L}} can be inhibited by \textit{Cdk1} activity if either \textit{BCL2}, \textit{MCL-1}, or \textit{Plk1} are OFF. In the absence of \textit{Plk1}, loss of either \textit{BCL2} or \textit{MCL-1} can result in \textit{Bcl-x\textsubscript{L}} inhibition (even without \textit{Cdk1} phosphorylation), as we assume its targets are no longer competitively bound by its family members.

While the precise combinatorial logic governing \textit{BCL2} activity is not clear from literature, we modeled \textit{BCL2} as ON in the absence of \textit{Caspase 3}, \textit{BAD}, \textit{BIM} or \textit{BIK}. This choice makes \textit{BCL2} the most sensitive of the three family members to activation of its three inhibitors. In addition, mitotic \textit{BCL2} is blocked by \textit{Cdk1} if both \textit{BCL-xL} and \textit{MCL-1} are OFF. In the absence of \textit{Plk1}, loss of either \textit{BCL2} or \textit{MCL-1} can result in \textit{BCL-2} inhibition (even without \textit{Cdk1} phosphorylation), as we assume its targets are no longer competitively bound by its family members.

\textit{BAD} in our model is ON when cleaved by \textit{Caspase 3}, or in the complete absence of survival signals (\textit{AKT}, \textit{ERK} or \textit{S6K}). Alternatively, \textit{BAD} can be cleaved and activated by \textit{Caspase 8} in the absence of strong survival signaling. We modeled this inhibitory survival signal as either the combined activity of \textit{ERK}, \textit{S6K} and (at least) basal \textit{AKT}, or high \textit{AKT} in the joint presence of ERK and basal \textit{AKT} (indicating that \textit{AKT\_H} will not drop by the next time-step).

\textit{BIK} is free to activate its target, \textit{BAX}, only when it is not sequestered by any of the three \textit{BCL-2} family proteins \cite{gelinasBH3onlyProteinsControl2005} {and it is either induced by \textit{SMADs} \cite{spenderTGFbetaInducesApoptosis2009} or protected by no more than basal \textit{AKT} activity, which lowers the level of both \textit{BCL2} and \textit{BCL-x\textsubscript{L}} \cite{jacquinGAPDHBindsActive2013}}.

\textit{BIM}’s pro-apoptotic activity requires expression driven by \textit{FoxO3} and aided by \textit{GSK3}, as well as the absence of \textit{ERK} or any of the three inhibitory \textit{BCL2} family proteins. {Alternatively, \textit{Runx1} can induce BIM to apoptotic levels in the absence of \textit{ERK} and \textit{NF-$\kappa$B}, assuming the three inhibitory \textit{BCL2} family proteins are not all fully active.}

\textit{BID} is truncated in response to \textit{Caspase 8} activation. In addition, \textit{Caspase 2} can also promote \textit{BID} activation once all three pro-apoptotic \textit{BCL2} family proteins are blocked.

Given that \textit{BAK} is preferentially activated by \textit{BID} compared to \textit{BIM} \cite{sarosiekBIDPreferentiallyActivates2013} and that it is less responsive to sequestration by \textit{BCL2} than the other two anti-apoptotic \textit{BCL2} family proteins \cite{zhaiDifferentialRegulationBax2008,willisProapoptoticBakSequestered2005}, \textit{BAK} in our model turns on when stimulated by \textit{BID} if one or more \textit{BCL2} family proteins are absent, or if \textit{BIM} or \textit{BIK} are also present. In contrast, \textit{BIM} or \textit{BIK} only activate \textit{BAK} if \textit{BCL-xL} and \textit{MCL-1} are absent (\textit{BCL-2} alone cannot block them).

In contrast to \textit{BAK}, \textit{BAX} is preferentially activated by \textit{BIM} compared to \textit{BID} \cite{sarosiekBIDPreferentiallyActivates2013} and it is less responsive to sequestration by \textit{MCL-1} than the other two anti-apoptotic BCL2 family proteins \cite{zhaiDifferentialRegulationBax2008,willisProapoptoticBakSequestered2005}. \textit{BAX} in our model turns on when stimulated by \textit{BIM} if one or more \textit{BCL2} family proteins are absent, or if \textit{BID} or \textit{BIK} are also present. In contrast, \textit{BID} or \textit{BIK} only activate \textit{BAK} if \textit{BCL2} and \textit{BCL-xL} are both absent (\textit{MCL-1} alone cannot block them).
\textit{Cytochrome C} release from mitochondria requires the oligomerization of either \textit{BAK} or \textit{BAX} \cite{weiProapoptoticBAXBAK2001}.
\textit{SMAC/Diablo} release from mitochondria requires the oligomerization of either \textit{BAK} or \textit{BAX} \cite{weiProapoptoticBAXBAK2001,zhouDynamicsStructureBaxBak2008}.

Inhibitor of Apoptosis Proteins (\textit{IAP}s) are active in the absence of \textit{SMAC} inhibition, or following \textit{AKT\_H} mediated upregulation (this protection from \textit{SMAC} requires peak or oncogenic \textit{AKT} activity). {\color{NavyBlue}Under hypoxia, \textit{IAP-2} levels are increased by a \textit{Hif-1$\alpha$} independent mechanism \cite{dongUpregulationApoptosisInhibitory2001}; a process we assume requires at least basal levels of \textit{AKT}.}

\textit{Procaspase 9} is cleaved into active \textit{Caspase 9} by \textit{Caspase 3}, or by the apoptosome (which relies on \textit{cytochrome C} for its assembly) in the absence of \textit{IAP} proteins.

Activation of \textit{Caspase 3} requires proteolytic cleavage of \textit{procaspase-3} by initiator caspases such as \textit{Caspase 9} or \textit{Caspase 8}. In our model, cooperation of two of the three caspases (\textit{Casp9}, \textit{Casp8}, \textit{Casp3}) is required in the presence of \textit{IAP}s, which inhibit the proteolytic activity of \textit{Caspase 3} by bind tightly to its active site. In the absence of \textit{IAP}s, either of the three caspases can cleave and activate \textit{Caspase 3}.

Caspase-activated DNase (\textit{CAD}) is activated when its inhibition is released via the cleavage of \textit{ICAD} (inhibitor of caspase-activated DNase). While \textit{Capsase 3} and \textit{7} (a direct target of \textit{Caspase 9}) can inhibit \textit{ICAD} \cite{wolfCaspase3PrimaryActivator1999}, in our model they are both required, as \textit{CAD} = ON is represents terminal, irreversible apoptotic commitment, which is fully locked in when both \textit{Caspase 3} and \textit{9} are on.
